sources.design: nine populations across a snowmelt/flowering gradient; 2017-2019

published_numeric_results.late_population_predation_description: no predation damage reported for the late end of the phenological gradient

sources.interpretation: Within-population predation was driven primarily by phenological exposure rather than flower-number preference, while populations experiencing recurrent high predation were consistently more male-biased. This is a geographic selection-mosaic / allocation pattern, not a causal dimensional-release experiment.

sources.design: five plots across a flowering gradient, 2020-2023, plus a 2021 high-predation focal experiment and paternity analysis
published_directional_results_without_nu: predator moths tended to oviposit on umbels with more perfect flowers, fewer male flowers and taller stems
greater total flower production increased siring success whereas perfect-flower production itself did not
male-flower production was negatively related to oviposition preference
selection on perfect-flower production shifted from negative in high-predation early populations to positive in low-predation late populations
sources.interpretation: The later study closes key functional pieces missing in 2021: perfect flowers contribute to female opportunity but expose seeds to predation, whereas shifting allocation toward male flowers can retain/display male function while reducing the seed-bearing target. This supports partial functional differentiation and a context-dependent selection mosaic, but not canonical R_state.
